title: A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks

hero.subtitle: The standard that married IP to Ethernet — defining how datagrams become frames

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 894 defines how Internet Protocol (IP) datagrams are encapsulated for transmission over Ethernet networks. This deceptively simple standard is one of the most consequential in networking history — it is the reason IP and Ethernet work together.

Every time an IP packet leaves a host on an Ethernet LAN, it is framed according to this specification. The standard has remained essentially unchanged since 1984, a testament to its elegant simplicity.

The specification defines three key things: the Ethernet type field value for IP (0x0800), the mapping of IP datagrams into Ethernet frame payloads, and the handling of the 46-byte minimum frame size through padding.
sections.eli5: Think of the Internet as a letter and the Ethernet as the postal van. This page says exactly how to put the letter into the van's envelope so any van driver understands it. Because everyone follows the same recipe, a letter written on one computer can ride the van of another company.

sections.title: Frame Format
sections.content:
IP Datagram in an Ethernet Frame
+---------------------------+
| Destination Address (6)   |
+---------------------------+
| Source Address (6)        |
+---------------------------+
| Type = 0x0800 (2)         |
+---------------------------+
|                           |
|      IP Datagram          |
|    (46 - 1500 bytes)      |
|                           |
+---------------------------+
| Frame Check Sequence (4)  |
+---------------------------+
Destination Address48-bit Ethernet address of the destination host or broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)6 bytes
Source Address48-bit Ethernet address of the sending host6 bytes
Type FieldSet to 0x0800 to identify the payload as an IP datagram2 bytes
Data (IP Datagram)The IP datagram, padded to 46 bytes if necessary46–1500 bytes
Frame Check SequenceCRC-32 for error detection4 bytes
sections.eli5: The envelope has an address for who gets it, an address for who sent it, and a small label saying "this contains an Internet message". Inside goes the message itself. If the message is tiny, you add blank paper so the envelope is never too thin.

sections.title: Encapsulation Rules
sections.content:
The rules for encapsulating IP datagrams in Ethernet frames are straightforward but important:

Maximum Transmission Unit
The maximum length of an IP datagram sent over Ethernet is 1500 bytes. This defines the Ethernet MTU and is one of the most fundamental constants in networking. IP datagrams larger than this must be fragmented.
Minimum Frame Size
Ethernet requires a minimum frame size of 64 bytes (excluding preamble). Since the header is 14 bytes and the FCS is 4 bytes, the data field must be at least 46 bytes. Short IP datagrams are padded with octets of zero.
Type Field Identification
The EtherType value 0x0800 identifies the frame as carrying an IP datagram. This distinguishes IP traffic from ARP (0x0806), RARP (0x8035), and other protocols on the same Ethernet.
Byte Order
As described in Appendix B of the IP specification (RFC 791), the IP datagram is transmitted over the Ethernet as a series of 8-bit bytes.
sections.eli5: There are a few rules about size and labels. The message cannot be longer than 1500 pieces, a short one gets padded with zeros, and the label "0800" tells the receiver it is an Internet message, not some other kind of mail.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
Translating between 32-bit IP addresses and 48-bit Ethernet addresses requires the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP):

ARP for Unicast
When sending to a specific host on the local network, the sender uses ARP (RFC 826) to resolve the destination IP address to its Ethernet MAC address.
Broadcast Mapping
IP broadcast datagrams (destination 255.255.255.255 or subnet broadcast) are sent to the Ethernet broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF.
IP EtherType0x0800
ARP EtherType0x0806
Ethernet MTU1500 bytes
Min Data Field46 bytes
Broadcast AddrFF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF

The 1500-byte MTU defined by this standard has persisted for over 40 years and remains the default MTU on virtually all Ethernet networks, making it one of the most enduring constants in Internet engineering.
sections.eli5: Internet addresses are like street names and Ethernet addresses are like the number on each house door. To deliver, a computer needs to know which door goes with which street name. It can look it up in a list or just shout and ask, and shouting (ARP) is the favored way.

references.text: Plummer, D., "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol", RFC 826, November 1982.
Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, "A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over IEEE 802 Networks", RFC 1042, February 1988.

subtitle: The standard that married IP to Ethernet, defining how datagrams become frames.

tldr.problem: IP datagrams need one agreed way to travel inside Ethernet frames so that hosts from different vendors can talk.
tldr.mechanism: The datagram goes in the frame's data field with the Ethernet type field set to hexadecimal 0800, padded with zero octets to at least 46 octets, and ARP maps IP addresses to Ethernet addresses.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 still rides on Ethernet this way, and the 1500-octet limit is still the default Ethernet MTU.

eli5.summary: This is the rule for putting an Internet message into an Ethernet envelope: write the right label on the front, make sure the message is not too short, and never make it longer than 1500 pieces.

questions: how are ip packets sent over ethernet
why is the ethernet mtu 1500 bytes
why must an ethernet payload be at least 46 bytes
how does ip broadcast map to ethernet
today: Almost every IPv4 packet that crosses an Ethernet link is still framed this way: EtherType 0x0800, a payload of up to 1500 octets, and zero padding for short packets. The 1500-octet limit is still the default MTU on Ethernet interfaces, which is why path MTU discovery and TCP's maximum segment size option matter. Trailer encapsulation, the BSD 4.2 optional format the RFC mentions, has long since disappeared.
